claim: N-glycan modifying a large number of proteins that enter the ER is converted from oligomannose type to complex type in the Golgi.
source: N-Glycan modifying a large number of proteins that enter the ER is converted from oligomannose type to complex type in the Golgi and is deeply involved in biological phenomena inside and outside the cell (Pinho et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pinho et al., 2023, which provides external scholarly support for this statement.

claim: The N-glycan added to nascent proteins is composed of three glucose, nine mannoses, and two N-acetylglucosamines (GlcNAc), and is termed Glc3Man9GlcNAc2 (G3M9).
source: The N-glycan added to nascent proteins is composed of three glucose, nine mannoses, and two N-acetylglucosamines (GlcNAc), and is termed Glc3Man9GlcNAc2 (G3M9), which is processed to GM9 by the actions of glucosidase I and glucosidase II.
evidence: This is established knowledge about N-glycan structure and processing in the ER.

claim: Calnexin (CNX) and calreticulin (CRT) recognize glycoproteins with GM9 to facilitate productive folding.
source: Calnexin (CNX) and calreticulin (CRT) recognize glycoproteins with GM9 to facilitate productive folding (Lamriben et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lamriben et al., 2016.

claim: UGGT1 promotes substrate solubility.
source: UGGT1 promotes substrate solubility (Ferris et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ferris et al., 2013.

claim: UGGT1 prefers proteins with exposed hydrophobic regions to folded proteins.
source: UGGT1 promotes substrate solubility (Ferris et al., 2013) and prefers proteins with exposed hydrophobic regions to folded proteins (Caramelo et al., 2004; Sousa and Parodi, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Caramelo et al., 2004 and Sousa and Parodi, 1995.

claim: UGGT2's glucosyltransferase activity is weaker than that of UGGT1 at least in humans.
source: UGGT1 has a paralogue, UGGT2, whose glucosyltransferase activity is weaker than that of UGGT1 at least in humans (Ito et al., 2020; Takeda et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ito et al., 2020 and Takeda et al., 2014.

claim: Mannose residues are trimmed from M9 first by EDEM2-S-S-TXNDC11 complex to M8B.
source: If glycoproteins with M9 are not folded correctly within a certain period, mannose residues are trimmed from M9 first by EDEM2-S-S-TXNDC11 complex to M8B (George et al., 2020; Ninagawa et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to George et al., 2020 and Ninagawa et al., 2014.

claim: Mannose residues are trimmed by EDEM3/1 to M7A, M6 and M5 exposing α1,6-bonded mannose on the glycoproteins.
source: mannose residues are trimmed from M9 first by EDEM2-S-S-TXNDC11 complex to M8B (George et al., 2020; Ninagawa et al., 2014) and then by EDEM3/1 to M7A, M6 and M5 exposing α1,6-bonded mannose on the glycoproteins (George et al., 2021; Hirao et al., 2006; Ninagawa et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to George et al., 2021, Hirao et al., 2006, and Ninagawa et al., 2014.

claim: Glycoproteins with trimmed mannoses exposing α1,6-bonded mannose are recognized by OS9 or XTP3B lectins for degradation.
source: and then by EDEM3/1 to M7A, M6 and M5 exposing α1,6-bonded mannose on the glycoproteins (George et al., 2021; Hirao et al., 2006; Ninagawa et al., 2014), which are recognized by OS9 or XTP3B lectins for degradation (van der Goot et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to van der Goot et al., 2018.

claim: The presence of one glucose in the A branch of N-glycans did not change the timing of substrate degradation in MI8-5 Chinese hamster ovary cells.
source: MI8-5 Chinese hamster ovary cells are deficient in the dolichol-P-glucose–dependent glycosyltransferase termed Alg6, and therefore produce only glycoproteins with N-glycans lacking glucoses (M9). In these cells, N-glycans with one glucose are produced only by the action of UGGTs. Accordingly, the monoglucosylated state is maintained by treatment of MI8-5 with the glucosidase inhibitor 1-deoxynojirimycin (DNJ). It was found that such trapping of glycoproteins in a monoglucosylated state delayed their efflux from the ER, as expected, but did not affect their rate of degradation.
evidence: This is a description of previously published findings from Tannous et al., 2015, as indicated in the preceding text.

claim: The growth rate of UGGT1-KO, UGGT2-KO, and UGGT-DKO cell populations was not significantly altered compared to wild-type cells.
source: The growth rate of the KO cell population was not significantly altered (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C, which displays doubling times for different cell lines.

claim: The protein expression level of UGGT2 in HCT116 cells is approximately 4.5% of that of UGGT1.
source: In our hands, the protein expression levels of UGGT2 in HCT116 and HeLa cells were found to be approximately 4.5% and 26% of that of UGGT1, respectively, as estimated by transfection of UGGT1-Myc3 and UGGT2-Myc3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The protein expression level of UGGT2 in HeLa cells is approximately 26% of that of UGGT1.
source: In our hands, the protein expression levels of UGGT2 in HCT116 and HeLa cells were found to be approximately 4.5% and 26% of that of UGGT1, respectively, as estimated by transfection of UGGT1-Myc3 and UGGT2-Myc3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: ER stress marker proteins BiP, XBP1(S), and ATF4 were not induced in UGGT1-KO, UGGT2-KO, or UGGT-DKO cells.
source: Immunoblotting showed that ER stress marker proteins BiP, XBP1(S), and ATF4 were not induced in UGGT1-KO, UGGT2-KO, or UGGT-DKO cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Both UGGT1 and UGGT2 are modified with N-glycans.
source: Both UGGT1 and UGGT2 are modified with N-glycans, as indicated by their sensitivity to treatment with Endoglycosidase H (EndoH), which cleaves oligomannose-type N-glycans localized in the ER (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by EndoH treatment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: In UGGT1-KO and UGGT-DKO cells but not in UGGT2-KO cells, the secretion efficiency of α1-antitrypsin (A1AT) and erythropoietin (EPO) was decreased.
source: In UGGT1-KO and UGGT-DKO cells but not in UGGT2-KO cells, the secretion efficiency of α1-antitrypsin (A1AT) and erythropoietin (EPO) determined by pulse-chase experiments using 35S was decreased (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, E).
evidence: The claim is supported by pulse-chase experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D and E.

claim: In UGGTs-KO cells, maturation of hemagglutinin (HA) from oligomannose type to complex type was delayed.
source: In UGGTs-KO cells, maturation of hemagglutinin (HA) from oligomannose type to complex type was delayed, as reported previously (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F; Hung et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F and a citation to Hung et al., 2022.

claim: ATF6α functions as an unfolded protein response (UPR) sensor/transducer but is a somewhat unfolded protein that is constitutively subjected to gpERAD.
source: We previously showed that ATF6α functions as an unfolded protein response (UPR) sensor/transducer but is a somewhat unfolded protein that is constitutively subjected to gpERAD (Haze et al., 1999; Horimoto et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Haze et al., 1999 and Horimoto et al., 2013.

claim: The half-life of ATF6α in WT HCT116 cells was less than 2 hr.
source: The half-life of ATF6α in WT HCT116 cells was less than 2 hr and degradation of ATF6α was blocked almost completely in SEL1L-KO cells (the construction and characterization of these KO cells is described in Figure 1—figure supplement 3) and in EDEM1/2/3-triple KO (TKO) HCT116 cells (Figure 1D)
evidence: The claim is supported by cycloheximide chase data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Degradation of ATF6α was blocked almost completely in SEL1L-KO cells and in EDEM1/2/3-triple KO (TKO) HCT116 cells.
source: The half-life of ATF6α in WT HCT116 cells was less than 2 hr and degradation of ATF6α was blocked almost completely in SEL1L-KO cells (the construction and characterization of these KO cells is described in Figure 1—figure supplement 3) and in EDEM1/2/3-triple KO (TKO) HCT116 cells (Figure 1D), as was shown previously (Horimoto et al., 2013; Ninagawa et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D and citations to Horimoto et al., 2013 and Ninagawa et al., 2014.

claim: The degradation of ATF6α was markedly accelerated in UGGT1-KO and UGGT-DKO cells but not in UGGT2-KO cells.
source: Strikingly, the degradation of ATF6α was markedly accelerated in UGGT1-KO and UGGT-DKO cells but not in UGGT2-KO cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by cycloheximide chase data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: UGGT1 is involved in ERAD.
source: These findings revealed for the first time that UGGT1 is involved in ERAD.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing accelerated degradation in UGGT1-KO cells.

claim: ATF6α was stabilized in UGGT-DKO cells treated with a mannosidase inhibitor, kifunensine, indicating that the acceleration of ATF6α degradation still required mannose trimming.
source: The fact that ATF6α was stabilized in UGGT-DKO cells treated with a mannosidase inhibitor, kifunensine, as in WT cells treated with kifunensine, indicated that the acceleration of ATF6α degradation still required mannose trimming (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by cycloheximide chase data with kifunensine treatment shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Treatment of WT cells with DNJ did not affect the degradation rate of ATF6α.
source: Treatment of WT cells with DNJ did not affect the degradation rate of ATF6α (Figure 1D, middle panel), consistent with the previously published claim described in the Introduction.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: Accumulation of GM9 rather than G3M9 or G2M9 was observed in WT, UGGT-DKO, and EDEM-TKO cells after treatment with DNJ.
source: Indeed, accumulation of GM9 rather than G3M9 or G2M9 was observed in WT, UGGT-DKO, and EDEM-TKO cells after treatment with DNJ [Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–C (raw data), Figure 1—figure supplement 5A–C (isomer composition ratio)].
evidence: The claim is supported by N-glycan profiling data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–C and Figure 1—figure supplement 5A–C.

claim: The accelerated degradation of ATF6α in UGGT-DKO cells was compromised by treatment with DNJ, so that the degradation rate of ATF6α became very similar in WT and UGGT-DKO cells after treatment with DNJ.
source: Treatment of WT cells with DNJ resulted in a similar degradation rate of ATF6α, however, the accelerated degradation of ATF6α in UGGT-DKO cells was compromised by treatment with DNJ, so that the degradation rate of ATF6α became very similar in WT and UGGT-DKO cells after treatment with DNJ (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by cycloheximide chase data with DNJ treatment shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The glucose trimming-mediated production rate of M9 is important for efficient gpERAD.
source: This implies that the glucose trimming-mediated production rate of M9 is important for efficient gpERAD.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that DNJ treatment affects degradation rates differently in WT and UGGT-DKO cells.

claim: An increase in the level of GM9 and the decrease in the level of M9 were observed in WT and UGGT-DKO cells treated with DNJ.
source: Indeed, an increase in the level of GM9 and the decrease in the level of M9 were observed in WT and UGGT-DKO cells treated with DNJ [Figure 1—figure supplement 4A, B (raw data) and Figure 1—figure supplement 5A, B (isomer composition ratio)].
evidence: The claim is supported by N-glycan profiling data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A, B and Figure 1—figure supplement 5A, B.

claim: Mannose trimming still occurred even in the absence of glucose trimming, as evidenced by the increased detection of GM8 in WT and UGGT-DKO cells treated with DNJ.
source: We consider it likely that this is because mannose trimming still occurred even in the absence of glucose trimming, as evidenced by the increased detection of GM8 in WT and UGGT-DKO cells treated with DNJ [Figure 1—figure supplement 4A, B (raw data) Figure 1—figure supplement 5A, B (isomer composition rate)]
evidence: The claim is supported by N-glycan profiling data showing GM8 detection in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A, B and Figure 1—figure supplement 5A, B.

claim: The active role of UGGT1 in gpERAD was demonstrated for the first time by the gene knockout strategy.
source: As the occurrence of mannose trimming in the presence of DNJ (GM9 >GM8>GM7) obscured the effect of reglucosylation on gpERAD in a previous study (Tannous et al., 2015), the active role of UGGT1 in gpERAD was demonstrated here for the first time by our gene knockout strategy.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results using UGGT1-KO cells, contrasting with previous studies using inhibitors.

claim: UGGT1-mediated reglucosylation reduces the probability of the mannose trimming that is a prerequisite for gpERAD.
source: We consider that UGGT1-mediated reglucosylation reduces the probability of the mannose trimming that is a prerequisite for gpERAD.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations about the effects of UGGT1 knockout on degradation rates.

claim: The degradation of NHK was accelerated in UGGT1-KO and UGGT-DKO cells but not in UGGT2-KO cells.
source: We found that the degradation of NHK was accelerated in UGGT1-KO and UGGT-DKO cells but not in UGGT2-KO cells (Figure 2A), similar to the case of ATF6α.
evidence: The claim is supported by pulse-chase experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The acceleration of NHK degradation in UGGT1-KO cells required glucosyltransferase activity.
source: Of note, this acceleration required glucosyltransferase activity, as introduction of myc-tagged WT UGGT1 but not its catalytically inactive mutant, D1358A located in the DxD motif (Takeda et al., 2014), into UGGT1-KO cells by transfection decelerated the degradation of NHK (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 2B and a citation to Takeda et al., 2014.

claim: The degradation rate of NHK-QQQ, in which all three N-glycosylation sites in NHK were mutated, was not affected by gene disruption of UGGT1 or UGGT2.
source: Accordingly, the degradation rate of NHK-QQQ, in which all three N-glycosylation sites in NHK were mutated (Ninagawa et al., 2015), was not affected by gene disruption of UGGT1 or UGGT2 (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by pulse-chase data shown in Figure 2C and a citation to Ninagawa et al., 2015.

claim: Simultaneous overexpression of Myc-CNX and Myc-UGGT1 significantly retarded NHK degradation.
source: We found that simultaneous overexpression of Myc-CNX and Myc-UGGT1 significantly retarded NHK degradation (Figure 2D)
evidence: The claim is supported by pulse-chase data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Simultaneous overexpression of EDEM2 and EDEM3 accelerated NHK degradation.
source: while simultaneous overexpression of EDEM2 and EDEM3 accelerated NHK degradation (Figure 2E, right top panel), as previously reported (Hirao et al., 2006; Mast et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by pulse-chase data shown in Figure 2E and citations to Hirao et al., 2006 and Mast et al., 2005.

claim: The accelerated degradation of NHK by EDEM2 and EDEM3 overexpression was compromised by co-overexpression of Myc-CNX and Myc-UGGT1.
source: Importantly, such accelerated degradation of NHK was compromised by co-overexpression of Myc-CNX and Myc-UGGT1 (Figure 2E, right bottom panel), revealing a tug of war between the CNX/CRT cycle and gpERAD.
evidence: The claim is supported by pulse-chase data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: There is a tug of war between the CNX/CRT cycle and gpERAD.
source: Importantly, such accelerated degradation of NHK was compromised by co-overexpression of Myc-CNX and Myc-UGGT1 (Figure 2E, right bottom panel), revealing a tug of war between the CNX/CRT cycle and gpERAD.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the competition experiments showing that CNX/UGGT1 can counteract EDEM-mediated degradation.

claim: ER-localized endogenous proteins Grp170, Sil1, and ribophorin I were stable both in WT and in UGGT-DKO cells.
source: We examined the effect of UGGT1/2 knockout on the stability of ER-localized endogenous proteins and found that they were stable both in WT and in UGGT-DKO cells no matter whether they were glycoproteins (Grp170, Sil1, and ribophorin I) or non-glycoproteins (CRT) (Figure 3A–D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by cycloheximide chase data shown in Figure 3A–D.

claim: The activity of the Golgi-resident glycosyltransferase GnT-V (MGAT5) was similar in WT, UGGT1-KO, UGGT2-KO and UGGT-DKO cells.
source: Similarly, the activity of the Golgi-resident glycosyltransferase GnT-V (MGAT5) with six putative N-glycosylation sites (Hirata et al., 2023) was similar in WT, UGGT1-KO, UGGT2-KO and UGGT-DKO cells (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by GnT-V activity assay data shown in Figure 3E and a citation to Hirata et al., 2023.

claim: A truncated version of rat ribophorin I lacking its C-terminal region (aa333-606), termed rRI332-Flag, was unstable in WT cells compared with ribophorin I when expressed by transfection.
source: Interestingly, a truncated version of rat ribophorin I lacking its C-terminal region (aa333-606), termed rRI332-Flag, (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; de Virgilio et al., 1998; Mueller et al., 2006) was unstable in WT cells compared with ribophorin I when expressed by transfection
evidence: The claim is supported by pulse-chase data shown in Figure 3D and citations to de Virgilio et al., 1998 and Mueller et al., 2006.

claim: The degradation rate of rRI332-Flag was accelerated in UGGT1-KO and UGGT-DKO cells but not in UGGT2-KO cells.
source: and its degradation rate was accelerated in UGGT1-KO and UGGT-DKO cells but not in UGGT2-KO cells (Figure 3D, right panel), similar to ATF6α and NHK.
evidence: The claim is supported by pulse-chase data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: EMC1 is a type I transmembrane protein with three N-glycosylation sites, and is involved in the insertion of membrane proteins into the ER membrane.
source: EMC1 is a type I transmembrane protein with three N-glycosylation sites, and is involved in the insertion of membrane proteins into the ER membrane (Jonikas et al., 2009; Shurtleff et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jonikas et al., 2009 and Shurtleff et al., 2018.

claim: Endogenous EMC1 was a relatively stable protein in both WT and UGGT-DKO cells.
source: Endogenous EMC1 was a relatively stable protein in both WT and UGGT-DKO cells
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The degradation rate of EMC1-ΔPQQ lacking the PQQ domain was accelerated in UGGT1-KO and UGGT-DKO cells but not in UGGT2-KO cells.
source: however, when EMC1-ΔPQQ lacking the PQQ domain was expressed by transfection, the degradation rate of EMC1-ΔPQQ was accelerated in UGGT1-KO and UGGT-DKO cells but not in UGGT2-KO cells (Figure 3F), similar to the case of ribophorin I vs rRI332-Flag.
evidence: The claim is supported by pulse-chase data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: UGGT1-mediated reglucosylation affects the fate of unstable proteins but not stable proteins.
source: Thus, UGGT1-mediated reglucosylation affects the fate of unstable proteins but not stable proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential effects of UGGT1 knockout on stable versus unstable protein variants.

claim: The protein expression level of endogenous ATF6α(P) was significantly decreased in UGGT1-KO and UGGT-DKO cells but not in UGGT2-KO cells.
source: Degradation of ATF6α(P) was accelerated in UGGT1-KO and UGGT-DKO cells but not in UGGT2-KO cells (Figure 1E), and accordingly, the protein expression level of endogenous ATF6α(P) was significantly decreased in UGGT1-KO and UGGT-DKO cells but not in UGGT2-KO cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The remaining ATF6α(P) in UGGT1-KO cells tended to have a more rigid structure that averts degradation, as suggested by its slightly lower sensitivity to trypsin.
source: We noticed conformational change in ATF6α(P), as the remaining ATF6α(P) in UGGT1-KO cells tended to have a more rigid structure that averts degradation, as suggested by its slightly lower sensitivity to trypsin (Figure 4B); a trypsin digestion assay can evaluate the rigidity of the protein structure (George et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2016; Ninagawa et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by trypsin digestion assay data shown in Figure 4B and citations to George et al., 2020, Liu et al., 2016, and Ninagawa et al., 2015.

claim: The amount of ATF6α(N) was significantly decreased in UGGT1-KO and UGGT-DKO cells but not in UGGT2-KO cells compared with WT cells after the treatment with thapsigargin.
source: The amount of ATF6α(N) was significantly decreased in UGGT1-KO and UGGT-DKO cells but not in UGGT2-KO cells compared with WT cells after the treatment with thapsigargin (Tg), an inhibitor of the ER calcium pump, which thereby induces ER stress (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4C–E.

claim: In WT cells, the ERSE and UPRE reporters were induced 4.8 and 12.1-fold by Tg treatment, respectively.
source: In WT cells, the ERSE and UPRE reporters were induced 4.8 and 12.1-fold by Tg treatment, respectively, and such induction was abolished in ATF6α-KO cells, as expected
evidence: The claim is supported by reporter assay data shown in Figure 4F–H.

claim: The induction of ERSE and UPRE reporters by Tg treatment was abolished in ATF6α-KO cells.
source: In WT cells, the ERSE and UPRE reporters were induced 4.8 and 12.1-fold by Tg treatment, respectively, and such induction was abolished in ATF6α-KO cells, as expected
evidence: The claim is supported by reporter assay data shown in Figure 4F–H.

claim: The ATF4 reporter was induced similarly in WT and ATF6α-KO cells.
source: whereas the ATF4 reporter was induced similarly in WT and ATF6α-KO cells (Figure 4F–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by reporter assay data shown in Figure 4F–H.

claim: In UGGT1-KO and UGGT-DKO cells, the induction level of the ERSE and UPRE reporters was significantly decreased in response to Tg treatment.
source: In UGGT1-KO and UGGT-DKO cells, the induction level of the ERSE and UPRE reporters was significantly decreased, whereas that of the ATF4 reporter was rather increased in response to Tg treatment (Figure 4F–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by reporter assay data shown in Figure 4F–H.

claim: In UGGT1-KO and UGGT-DKO cells, the induction level of the ATF4 reporter was rather increased in response to Tg treatment.
source: In UGGT1-KO and UGGT-DKO cells, the induction level of the ERSE and UPRE reporters was significantly decreased, whereas that of the ATF4 reporter was rather increased in response to Tg treatment (Figure 4F–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by reporter assay data shown in Figure 4F–H.

claim: UGGT1-KO and UGGT-DKO cells exhibited sensitivity to Tg treatment compared with WT cells.
source: Accordingly, UGGT1-KO and UGGT-DKO cells exhibited sensitivity to Tg treatment compared with WT cells (Figure 4I)
evidence: The claim is supported by crystal violet assay data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: UGGT1 is required for the proper functioning of ATF6α.
source: These results show that UGGT1 is required for the proper functioning of ATF6α.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data showing decreased ATF6α activity in UGGT1-KO cells.

claim: In WT cells, unfolded or misfolded glycoproteins with M9 are subjected to either the CNX/CRT cycle for folding via UGGT1-mediated reglucosylsation or gpERAD via EDEMs-mediated mannose trimming.
source: In WT cells, unfolded or misfolded glycoproteins with M9 are subjected to either the CNX/CRT cycle for folding via UGGT1-mediated reglucosylsation or gpERAD via EDEMs-mediated mannose trimming, leading to degradation at a certain rate [the half-life of ATF6α was ~1.5 hr (Figure 1E) and that of NHK was ~2.5 hr (Figure 2A)].
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental data shown in Figures 1E and 2A.

claim: In UGGT1-KO cells, unfolded or misfolded glycoproteins with M9 skip the CNX/CRT cycle and are subjected to gpERAD, resulting in accelerated degradation.
source: In UGGT1-KO cells, unfolded or misfolded glycoproteins with M9 skip the CNX/CRT cycle and are subjected to gpERAD, resulting in accelerated degradation [the half-life of ATF6α became less than 1 h (Figure 1E) and that of NHK became ~1.5 hr (Figure 2A)].
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental data shown in Figures 1E and 2A.

claim: Glycoproteins with stable conformational states do not require UGGT1.
source: Glycoproteins with stable conformational states do not require UGGT1, whereas unstable, unassembled, conformationally abnormal, or severely misfolded proteins are examined by UGGT1 for the possibility of proper folding in the CNX/CRT cycle.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential effects of UGGT1 knockout on stable versus unstable proteins.

claim: The capability of reglucosylation has an impact on determining the timing of substrate degradation, and UGGT1 acts to prevent early degradation.
source: Therefore, we conclude that the capability of reglucosylation has an impact on determining the timing of substrate degradation, and UGGT1 acts to prevent early degradation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations about the effects of UGGT1 on degradation timing.

claim: Substrate degradation was delayed by knockout of EDEMs.
source: Substrate degradation was delayed by knockout of EDEMs (George et al., 2020; Leto et al., 2019; Ninagawa et al., 2015; Ninagawa et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to George et al., 2020, Leto et al., 2019, Ninagawa et al., 2015, and Ninagawa et al., 2014.

claim: Substrate degradation was accelerated by overexpression of EDEMs.
source: and accelerated by overexpression of EDEMs (Figure 2E; Hirao et al., 2006; Mast et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E and citations to Hirao et al., 2006 and Mast et al., 2005.

claim: Substrate degradation was accelerated by knockout of UGGT1.
source: In contrast, substrate degradation was accelerated by knockout of UGGT1 (Figures 1E and 2A and Figure 3D–F)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1E, 2A, and 3D–F.

claim: Substrate degradation was delayed by overexpression of CNX and UGGT1.
source: and was delayed by overexpression of CNX and UGGT1 (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: UGGT1 plays a 'tug-of-war' with EDEMs regarding the determination of the fate of glycoproteins: whether to give them a chance to fold, or to degrade them.
source: It is further concluded that UGGT1 plays a 'tug-of-war' with EDEMs regarding the determination of the fate of glycoproteins: whether to give them a chance to fold, or to degrade them (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the competition experiments and is illustrated in Figure 5A.

claim: Mannose trimming is inefficient when a glucose residue is present on the A chain.
source: Nonetheless, as ATF6α was degraded at a similar rate in WT cells, WT cells treated with DNJ, and UGGT1-KO cells treated with DNJ (Figure 1G), we consider it likely that mannose trimming is inefficient when a glucose residue is present on the A chain (Figure 5).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that degradation rates are similar under these conditions, as shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The inhibitory effect of UGGT2 on substrate degradation appears to be quite limited in HCT116 cells.
source: Although it must be taken into account that the protein expression level of UGGT2 was markedly lower than that of UGGT1 in HCT116 compared to HeLa cells, the inhibitory effect of UGGT2 on substrate degradation appears to be quite limited in HCT116 cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that UGGT2-KO alone did not affect degradation rates.

claim: For all substrates used in this study, genetic disruption of UGGT2 alone did not accelerate degradation.
source: For all substrates used in this study, genetic disruption of UGGT2 alone did not accelerate degradation (Figures 1E and 2A and Figure 3D and F)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1E, 2A, and 3D and F.

claim: Overexpression of UGGT2 in UGGT-DKO cells did not attenuate the accelerated degradation of NHK, whereas overexpression of UGGT1 did so.
source: and overexpression of UGGT2 in UGGT-DKO cells did not attenuate the accelerated degradation of NHK, whereas overexpression of UGGT1 did so (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the text but the data is not shown.

claim: The loss of UGGT2 mitigated the transcriptional activity of ATF6α without affecting the ER stress-induced cleavage of ATF6α.
source: Instead, we found that the loss of UGGT2 mitigated the transcriptional activity of ATF6α (Figure 4F and G) without affecting the ER stress-induced cleavage of ATF6α (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D, F, and G.

claim: UGGT2 has been shown to decrease saturated fatty acids through lipid glucosylation.
source: Since UGGT2 has been shown to decrease saturated fatty acids through lipid glucosylation (Hung et al., 2022), lipid status may have some effect on the activity of ATF6α.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hung et al., 2022.

claim: UGGT1 is not just a CNX/CRT safety net, but should be considered to be a central component involved in the N-glycan-dependent folding and degradation in the ER.
source: Our findings strongly suggest that UGGT1 is not just a CNX/CRT safety net, but should be considered to be a central component involved in the N-glycan-dependent folding and degradation in the ER.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings showing UGGT1's role in both folding and degradation.

claim: The loss of UGGT1 reduced tolerance to ER stress in cultured cells.
source: The loss of UGGT1 reduced tolerance to ER stress in cultured cells (Figure 4I).
evidence: The claim is supported by crystal violet assay data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: UGGT1 is necessary for the proper functioning of ER-resident proteins such as ATF6α.
source: UGGT1 is necessary for the proper functioning of ER-resident proteins such as ATF6α (Figure 4C–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C–H.

claim: ATF6α undergoes structural maintenance by UGGT1, which would avoid unnecessary degradation and maintain proper function.
source: It is highly possible that ATF6α undergoes structural maintenance by UGGT1, which would avoid unnecessary degradation and maintain proper function, because ATF6α with a more rigid structure tended to remain in UGGT1-KO cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the trypsin digestion data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Responses of ERSE- and UPRE-containing promoters toward ER stress, which require ATF6α, were decreased in UGGT1-KO cells.
source: Responses of ERSE- and UPRE-containing promoters toward ER stress, which require ATF6α, were decreased in UGGT1-KO cells (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by reporter assay data shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: ATF4 reporter activity was increased in UGGT1-KO cells.
source: In contrast, ATF4 reporter activity was increased in UGGT1-KO cells (Figure 4H).
evidence: The claim is supported by reporter assay data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The ATF4 pathway might be activated to partially compensate for the functional loss of the ERSE and UPRE pathway in UGGT1-KO cells in response to acute ER stress.
source: Given that the basal expression level of ATF4 in UGGT1-KO cells was comparable to that in WT (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), the ATF4 pathway might be activated to partially compensate for the functional loss of the ERSE and UPRE pathway in UGGT1-KO cells in response to acute ER stress.
evidence: This is a speculative inference drawn from the observation of increased ATF4 reporter activity in UGGT1-KO cells.

claim: Saccharomyces cerevisiae does not have a functional orthologue of UGGT1.
source: Considering that Saccharomyces cerevisiae does not have a functional orthologue of UGGT1 (Ninagawa et al., 2021)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ninagawa et al., 2021.

claim: KO of UGGT1 causes embryonic lethality in mice.
source: and that KO of UGGT1 causes embryonic lethality in mice (Molinari et al., 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Molinari et al., 2005.

claim: UGGT1 is involved in the ER retention of Trop-2 mutant proteins, which are encoded by a causative gene of gelatinous drop-like corneal dystrophy.
source: Recently, it has been reported that UGGT1 is involved in the ER retention of Trop-2 mutant proteins, which are encoded by a causative gene of gelatinous drop-like corneal dystrophy (Tax et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tax et al., 2024.

claim: The ER is known to be involved in over 60 diseases.
source: Not only this, but since the ER is known to be involved in over 60 diseases (Guerriero and Brodsky, 2012), we must investigate how UGGT1 and other ER molecules are involved in diseases.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Guerriero and Brodsky, 2012.

claim: DNJ preferentially inhibits glucosidase II.
source: We then examined the effect of the glucosidase inhibitor DNJ, which preferentially inhibits glucosidase II (Saunier et al., 1982; Szumilo et al., 1987; Zeng et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Saunier et al., 1982, Szumilo et al., 1987, and Zeng et al., 1997.

claim: Castanospermine (CST) was reported to preferentially inhibit glucosidase I.
source: This notion was supported by the similar results obtained using another inhibitor of glucosidase I and II, castanospermine (CST) (Figure 1H), which was reported to preferentially inhibit glucosidase I (Saunier et al., 1982; Szumilo et al., 1987; Zeng et al., 1997)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Saunier et al., 1982, Szumilo et al., 1987, and Zeng et al., 1997.

claim: NHK is severely misfolded because of its C-terminus truncation resulting from TC deletion in the α1-antitrypsin (A1AT) gene.
source: NHK with three N-glycosylation sites is severely misfolded because of its C-terminus truncation resulting from TC deletion in the α1-antitrypsin (A1AT) gene (Sifers et al., 1988).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sifers et al., 1988.

claim: The glucosyltransferase activity of UGGT1 was required for the inhibition of early glycoprotein degradation.
source: An experiment with a point mutant of UGGT1 indicated that the glucosylation activity of UGGT1 was required for the inhibition of early glycoprotein degradation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The fate of glycoproteins is determined by a tug-of-war between structure formation by UGGT1 and degradation by EDEMs.
source: These and overexpression-based competition experiments suggested that the fate of glycoproteins is determined by a tug-of-war between structure formation by UGGT1 and degradation by EDEMs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: ATF6α cannot function properly without UGGT1.
source: We further demonstrated the physiological importance of UGGT1, since ATF6α cannot function properly without UGGT1.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: UGGT1 is a central factor in ER protein quality control via the regulation of both glycoprotein folding and degradation.
source: Thus, our work strongly suggests that UGGT1 is a central factor in ER protein quality control via the regulation of both glycoprotein folding and degradation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, supported by all the experimental data presented.

claim: UGGT1 delayed the degradation of misfolded substrates and unstable glycoproteins including ATF6α.
source: Strikingly, the results showed that UGGT1 delayed the degradation of misfolded substrates and unstable glycoproteins including ATF6α.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data shown in Figures 1E, 2A, and 3D-F.
